lead: Both readings are about waiting for the Lord’s coming. James tells his readers to be patient like a farmer who waits for the early and late rains, to stop grumbling at one another, and to take the prophets and Job as examples of endurance. In Mark, Jesus describes the day when the Son of Man will come in clouds with power and glory and gather his chosen ones from the four winds, and he tells the disciples to learn from the fig tree and to trust that his words will never pass away. The Church’s waiting is neither fear nor calculation but patient, watchful hope.

r.h: Be patient until the coming of the Lord
set: James has just warned the rich who oppress the poor (5:1–6). Now he turns to the poor and suffering believers, who may be tempted to take matters into their own hands or to complain against each other. His word to them is patience. The farmer’s picture suits the land of Israel: the early rains come in autumn and the late rains in spring, and the crop depends on both (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24).
str: vv. 7–8: be patient like the farmer until the coming of the Lord, which is near.
v. 9: do not grumble against one another; the Judge stands at the door.
vv. 10–11: the prophets and Job as examples of endurance; the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
v. 12: do not swear oaths; let your “Yes” be yes and your “No” be no.
kw: Literally to be “long of spirit”, slow to anger and slow to give up. The word is used of God’s own patience with sinners.
A steady holding on under pressure. Job is the model: he did not curse God even in his sorrow.
The word for the arrival of a king or the coming of Christ in glory. The early Christians prayed Maranatha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22).
vv: The farmer waits for the precious crop from the earth, being patient with it until it receives the early and the late rains.
The farmer works, but he cannot make the rain fall. A Christian also does what he can and leaves the harvest to God.
Beloved, do not grumble against one another, so that you may not be judged.
Complaining against each other is the first fruit of impatience. The Judge is already near, so there is no need to judge one another.
You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
The story of Job ends in God’s mercy, not in his silence. The words “compassionate and merciful” echo the name God gave himself in Exodus 34:6.
let your “Yes” be yes and your “No” be no
James echoes the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:34–37). A person of integrity needs no oath to be believed.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church awaits the Lord’s glorious return, which is certain though its day and hour are unknown (CCC 673–677). It also teaches that the Lord’s words about oaths do not forbid solemn oaths for grave and right reasons, as in a court of law, but call all Christians to truthfulness in ordinary speech (CCC 2150–2155). The Church has long held up Job’s endurance as a model for the sick and sorrowing, and the great commentary of St Gregory the Great, the Moralia on Job, shows how seriously the Fathers took the book.

r.h: The Son of Man coming in clouds
set: Jesus is on the Mount of Olives, looking across at the Temple, in the last days of his earthly life. Four disciples have asked him when the Temple will fall and what the sign will be (13:1–4). The whole chapter is an apocalyptic discourse: it speaks of wars, persecution and the destruction of Jerusalem, and then of the end of the age. The language of sun, moon and stars comes from the prophets (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10) and the scene of the Son of Man comes from Daniel 7:13–14. Such language is not a weather report but a way of saying that the order of the old world gives way to the reign of God.
Mark does not give a timetable. He gives a call to watch: the disciples are to read the signs as one reads the fig tree, with attention and without panic.
str: vv. 24–25: after the distress, the sun and moon are darkened and the powers of heaven are shaken.
v. 26: the Son of Man comes in clouds with great power and glory.
v. 27: he sends the angels to gather his elect from the four winds.
vv. 28–29: the lesson of the fig tree: when you see these things, know that he is near.
vv. 30–31: this generation will not pass away before all this happens; heaven and earth will pass, but my words will not.
kw: Those whom God has called and gathered, the whole people of God. The gathering from the “four winds” recalls God’s promise to bring home his scattered people (Deuteronomy 30:4; Zechariah 2:6).
Used of summer, and of the Lord. The Lord is near “at the very gates”. Nearness here is as much a matter of readiness as of time.
Can mean the people living at one time, or a kind of people. Verse 30 is one of the hardest in the Gospels (see below).
vv: Then they will see ‘the Son of Man coming in clouds’ with great power and glory.
Daniel’s vision of one like a son of man receiving the kingdom is now fulfilled in Jesus. The one who is about to be judged is the one who will come as Judge and King.
Then he will send out the angels, and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
The picture is not of terror but of gathering. The end is the final coming together of God’s scattered people.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have taken place.

Interpreters have understood this in different ways. Many hold that it refers to the generation that would see the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus describes as the first great sign of the end; others take “generation” as the whole people of faith, or take “all these things” as the signs that are the beginning. All agree that Jesus gives no date, as the next verse says (13:32).
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
The sure ground of hope is not the calendar but the word of Christ. Everything else may change; his promise will not.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s glorious return awaits the end of history and that the Church’s task is to watch and pray, for “about that day or hour no one knows” (CCC 668–677; Mark 13:32). It teaches that the Last Judgment will come when Christ returns in glory, and that God alone knows the hour (CCC 1040). The Church rejects any attempt to calculate the date. St Augustine, in a letter to Bishop Hesychius, wrote that Christians should not try to determine the time of the Lord’s coming but should live always ready for it (in substance, Letter 199).

qa: Does Jesus say the world will end in the lifetime of those who heard him?

Not in that sense. Mark’s Jesus says in the very next verse that nobody knows the day or hour, not even the Son (13:32). Verse 30 is explained by the Church in different ways, most often as a reference to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus speaks of as an early sign, or to the whole generation of those who see the signs begin. What is clear is that Christ calls his disciples to be ready every day.
study: James says the farmer waits for the early and the late rains. Where in my life must I wait patiently, doing what I can and leaving the rest to God?
Jesus says that his words will not pass away. Which of his words do I most need to hold on to this week?
